title: Compound Interest Explained: The 8th Wonder of the World
description:
Compound interest is the force that quietly makes some people rich and keeps others in debt for decades. In this video I explain it from three angles: the numbers (the rule of 72, a penny doubled for 30 days, Franklin's 200-year experiment), the psychology that makes our brains underestimate it, and a simple playbook to make it work for you instead of against you.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:57 How we got the numbers
2:30 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:36 1. Simple vs compound
3:57 2. The rule of 72
5:25 3. Compounding frequency
6:38 4. Adding money every month
7:50 5. Franklin's 200 year experiment
8:53 6. Buffett's late fortune
9:44 7. Compounding works against you
10:45 Angle 2: The Psychology
11:10 8. Exponential growth bias
12:35 9. The boring middle
13:52 10. Impatience
15:26 11. Present bias
16:42 12. Interruption is the enemy
17:59 13. The financial literacy gap
19:10 14. Small rates, big differences
20:32 Angle 3: The Playbook
20:49 15. Start now
21:50 16. Kill compounding debt
22:48 17. Reinvest everything
23:48 18. Lower your costs
24:42 19. Automate and ignore
25:41 20. Compound yourself too
26:38 Two savers
27:30 Compounding at every age
29:18 Questions people ask
32:05 Three compounding mistakes
33:15 Recap
33:54 What to do next

Sources:
- Quote Investigator, on the compound interest quote attributed to Albert Einstein (no reliable source)
- Historical accounts of Benjamin Franklin's 1790 bequests to Boston and Philadelphia
- Morgan Housel, The Psychology of Money (2020): Warren Buffett's net worth after age 65
- Stango and Zinman, Exponential Growth Bias and Household Finance (Journal of Finance, 2009)
- Lusardi and Mitchell, financial literacy questions (the Big Three)
- Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit (credit card rates above 20%)
- S&P Dow Jones Indices, dividends' share of S&P 500 total return
- Hershfield et al., Increasing Saving Behavior Through Age-Progressed Renderings of the Future Self (Journal of Marketing Research, 2011)
- Barber and Odean, Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth (Journal of Finance, 2000)
- S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Scorecard (active funds vs benchmarks)
- Charlie Munger: the first rule of compounding is never to interrupt it unnecessarily
- IRS, retirement plan and IRA catch-up contribution rules for age 50 and older
- Growth examples: compounding at stated average yearly returns (illustrations, not promises)
